Interconnection, L.L.C.'s (“PJM”) answer (“PJM Answer”)3 filed on March 24, 2025, in the above-
captioned docket.  Vistra appreciates the Commission’s acknowledgement of the urgency of the

It is critical for the Commission to direct PJM to accommodate Options 4 and 5

PJM’s Answer highlighted a number of other issues that warrant further attention.  Beyond Option 
4 and Option 5 configurations, PJM’s Answer identified other co-location configurations that 
PJM’s tariff does not yet accommodate, specifically Options 6-8 configurations.  Vistra supports 
further exploration of Options 6-8 to provide additional options and flexibility; there is significant 
interest in the industry to transact using these configurations.  As with Options 4-5, each of these 
configurations also could provide reliability and resource adequacy benefits.  However, they also 
appear likely to require more involved tariff modifications than those needed for Options 4 and 5.  
A triaging approach can help strike an appropriate balance between (a) resolving this proceeding 
with utmost speed, and (b) providing the flexibility to accommodate other beneficial co-location 
configurations.  Considering the possible outcomes of this proceeding illustrates the need for such 
a triaging approach.  On one extreme, PJM’s newfound approach of only allowing new large loads 
to interconnect under Options 1-2 would conclude this proceeding quickly, but it would also leave 
undue discrimination in place and result in significant litigation.  On the other extreme, the 
Commission could require PJM to implement tariff revisions to ensure its tariff accommodates all 
of Options 1-8, which would extend the length of this proceeding significantly.  The right balance 
is somewhere in the middle.  The Commission should act quickly to facilitate Options 4 and 5 in 
this proceeding, and direct PJM to conduct an expeditious stakeholder process regarding Options 
6-8.  This approach remedies the immediate undue discrimination without sacrificing the benefits 
of accommodating other potential co-location configurations.

The Commission need not wait until it has answers to every question raised in this

As a practical matter, it is imperative that the Commission recognize that time is of the

thereby fostering economic growth and national security benefits.  Thus, in deciding on an

I. 
Summary of Proposal 
In the below comments, Vistra suggests a specific replacement rate that the Commission 
could adopt quickly to ensure that the tariff accommodates Option 4 and 5 configurations in a just 
and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory manner.18  This proposal would ensure that co-
location configurations that fit within Options 4 and 5 pay their fair share and that other customers 
are not harmed.  Specifically, Vistra’s proposed solution includes the following components:   
 Clarify that transmission owners must cooperate in the necessary study process. 
 Ensure that co-location configurations pay their fair share by (a) allocating the costs 
of upgrades identified in the necessary study process to the generator, (b) creating 
a new rate design to ensure that Option 4 and 5 configurations pay for ancillary 
services that they use, or perhaps benefit from, but do not pay for services that they 
do not use or benefit from, and (c) when Option 5 configurations draw power from 
the grid, apply netting provisions consistent with the retail BTMG program. 
 Modify the pro forma ISA to include a co-location section that will govern the 
applicable data exchange and coordination requirements and formalize any 
requirements regarding applicable protective schemes. 
 Clarify that a secondary generator that provides occasional, interruptible backup 
service to a co-located load can also serve as a capacity resource because the 
generator will be available to PJM when needed.

II. 
Background 
In March 2024, as later revised in April 2024, PJM posted on its website a guidance

filed a petition for declaratory order regarding the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction over the 
interconnection of co-located load.21  On November 1, 2024, the Commission issued an order 
rejecting the proposed amendments to the Susquehanna ISA.22  On November 22, 2024, 
Constellation filed a complaint alleging that Exelon refused to review necessary studies to 
accommodate the addition of behind-the-meter co-located load at certain Constellation generating 
facilities.23

PJM’s Answer asserts that its tariff “remains just and reasonable” because it “permits co-

1 and 2 would be sufficient to render PJM’s tariff just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory.41  As discussed further below, requiring all new large loads to interconnect through 
Options 1 or 2 increases transmission costs for consumers and creates a structural bias in favor of 
transmission-served load while disadvantaging competitive, bilateral supply arrangements 
between sophisticated buyers and MBR sellers.  As discussed by Dr. Shanker, Option 4 and 5 
alternatives can avoid some of the delays and potential cost impacts to other consumers that result 
from Options 1 and 2 without any adverse impacts to resource adequacy or reliability.42  In fact, 
Options 4 and 5 can actually accrue benefits to existing load by decreasing costs and enhancing 
reliability.43

2. Co-located Load Should Pay its Fair Share—And No More
